title: The Sea Brings the First Arab Raids

title_i18n.en: The Sea Brings the First Arab Raids

subtitle: When Distant Winds Stir Vallabhi’s Shores
figure: Siladitya IV and Junayd ibn Abd al-Rahman
era: Umayyad pressure on western India, c. 636-740 CE
moral: Frontiers are defended by endurance as much as victory.

sources.citation: Al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan, trans. Philip Hitti (1916)
sources.note: Arabic narrative evidence for early raids on Bharuch and western India.

sources.citation: Khalid Yahya Blankinship, The End of the Jihad State (1994)
sources.note: Modern treatment of Umayyad campaigns including Junayd's Indian frontier.

sources.citation: Navsari grant of Avanijanashraya Pulakeshin, 739 CE
sources.note: Primary Indian evidence for the defeat of Arab forces in Gujarat by the Chalukya general.

panels.shot: sweeping wide of stormy Arabian Sea meeting Gujarat’s coast

dialogue.text: From the fall of Sindh to Navsari’s stand, Siladitya IV and Junayd ibn Abd al-Rahman face a century where the Arabian Sea becomes a frontier of fear and endurance.

panels.shot: wide aerial of trade routes across the Arabian Sea

dialogue.text: For centuries, the western coast of India traded across the Arabian Sea—spices, cloth and pearls carried by winds that knew no creed, only profit and courage.

panels.shot: slow push-in on bustling Bharuch port

dialogue.text: Bharuch, at the mouth of the Narmada, was a jewel in this web—a port whose wealth and position drew the gaze of distant rulers long before armies crossed the deserts.

panels.shot: dramatic interior of an Umayyad council hall in Damascus

dialogue.text: By 636, under the early Rashidun caliphs, Arab forces had begun to look east. The chronicles speak of raids by sea on Bharuch—testing India’s shores, not yet holding them.

panels.shot: low-angle on Arab raiding ships cutting through waves

dialogue.text: Al-Baladhuri’s Futuh al-Buldan preserves the memory: ships from the west struck Bharuch around 636–637, probing its defenses and disturbing a rhythm of trade centuries old.

panels.shot: tense wide of Bharuch’s shoreline under attack

dialogue.text: The sources do not linger on the faces in Bharuch that day, only on the blow to a port and its trade. A new pattern appeared: coastal raids for plunder and pressure, crossing the sea.

panels.shot: medium shot of Siladitya IV in Vallabhi’s court

dialogue.text: In Vallabhi, the Maitraka ruler Siladitya IV reigned in a world suddenly less certain—a world where reports of Arab raids and the later fall of Sindh shattered old assumptions of safety.

panels.shot: slow push-in on Siladitya IV’s contemplative profile

dialogue.text: Siladitya’s world was not defined by direct battles with Arab armies, but by disruption: ports under threat, trade unsettled, and the knowledge that distant powers could now reach his shores.

panels.shot: wide battlefield shot of Sindh under Arab attack

dialogue.text: In 711, the conquest of Sindh by Muhammad ibn al-Qasim opened a new gate. With Sindh under Umayyad control, Gujarat lay only a coast and a frontier away from their reach.

panels.shot: medium interior of Junayd ibn Abd al-Rahman’s frontier camp

dialogue.text: Decades later, under the Umayyads, Junayd ibn Abd al-Rahman governed Sindh. Blankinship’s study traces his campaigns that pushed toward Rajasthan and western India—more than raids, less than lasting rule.

panels.shot: split-scene style, Siladitya in Vallabhi and Junayd in Sindh

dialogue.text: They never faced each other in a single recorded battle. Yet Siladitya IV and Junayd shared a frontier: one defending a coastal kingdom, the other testing the limits of a rapidly grown empire.

panels.shot: wide shot of Gujarat’s forts and patrols on alert

dialogue.text: Gujarat’s rulers and their allies strengthened forts, guarded passes and watched the sea. Resistance here was not a single clash, but a long strain of preparation and wary vigilance.

panels.shot: epic aerial of the battlefield near Navsari

dialogue.text: The decisive break in this century of pressure came at Navsari in 739, where a Chalukya general, Avanijanashraya Pulakeshin, met the advancing Arab forces in open battle.

panels.shot: low-angle hero shot of Avanijanashraya Pulakeshin

dialogue.text: The Navsari grant of Avanijanashraya Pulakeshin, our chief Indian source, records that he repelled the Arab attack, preserving the region and earning titles that praised his stand.

panels.shot: dynamic wide of Indian forces pushing Arab lines back

dialogue.text: The inscription speaks of victory and a checked advance. It does not show the field, but its words mark a turning: after Navsari, Arab expansion deeper into Gujarat stalled.

panels.shot: reflective medium shot of Siladitya IV receiving news

dialogue.text: The sea brings danger, but also those who turn it back.

panels.shot: solemn close-up of Junayd reading reports in a tent

dialogue.text: Blankinship’s analysis shows the strain: overstretched lines, strong local powers, and defeats like Navsari made the Indian frontier costly for the Umayyads despite their earlier momentum.

panels.shot: wide montage of quieted ports and enduring forts

dialogue.text: In the years that followed, ports recovered, trade adapted, and frontier forts outlived the empires that strained against them. The sea remained a route of risk—and of resilience.

panels.shot: final contemplative wide of Siladitya IV overlooking the sea

dialogue.text: The record of Siladitya IV and Junayd ibn Abd al-Rahman on this frontier reminds us that borders are not only lines of sudden glory, but long years of endurance against distant tides.
